title: Consensus: Raft, Paxos, quorums, split brain
scopeHtml:
Scope: Quorums, split brain, Raft election and replication step by step, safety, reads, membership, Paxos intuition, production failure modes.

Scope: Quorums, split brain, Raft election and replication step by step, safety, reads, membership, Paxos intuition, production failure modes.

notes.title: What consensus solves
notes.html:
Consensus is getting several machines to agree on one value (or one ordered log of values), even when some machines crash and messages are delayed. Everything that needs "exactly one leader", "this config is the truth", or "this transaction order is final" ultimately rests on it.

Properties required:

  • Agreement: no two nodes decide different values.
  • Validity: the decided value was proposed by someone.
  • Termination (liveness): a decision is eventually reached if enough nodes work and the network is eventually stable.

The FLP result (1985) proves that in a fully asynchronous network no deterministic algorithm can guarantee all three if even one node may crash. Real algorithms (Raft, Paxos) keep safety always and give up guaranteed liveness: during network chaos they may stall, but they never decide wrongly.

Industry examples. etcd (Kubernetes' brain) uses Raft; ZooKeeper uses ZAB; Google Chubby and Spanner use Paxos; Consul uses Raft; CockroachDB runs one Raft group per data range; Kafka KRaft replaced ZooKeeper with a Raft-based controller quorum.

Everyday analogy. A committee deciding the meeting date by phone; some members may be unreachable, but once a majority agrees, the date is fixed and nobody can later claim a different one.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying consensus is needed for everything. Many systems (Dynamo-style, CRDTs) avoid it for availability.
  • Not knowing that consensus sacrifices availability on the minority side of a partition (CAP).

notes.title: Quorums and why majority
notes.html:
A quorum is the minimum number of nodes that must agree for a decision to count. A majority quorum is more than half: floor(N/2) + 1.

Why majority works: any two majorities of the same group share at least one node. So a newer decision must overlap the previous one and will learn about it. That overlap is the whole safety argument.

Cluster size N Majority Failures tolerated
3 2 1
4 3 1
5 3 2
7 4 3

Even sizes add cost but no fault tolerance (4 tolerates the same 1 as 3), so use odd sizes: 3 or 5. More nodes means slower writes (more acks) and more network chatter. etcd recommends 3 or 5 and warns that large clusters get slower.

Read/write quorums (Dynamo style): with N replicas, write quorum W and read quorum R, R + W > N guarantees reads overlap the latest write. N=3, W=2, R=2 is common. This is tunable quorum, different from strict consensus.

Worked example. A 5-node etcd cluster across 3 zones (2,2,1). Losing a whole zone of 2 leaves 3 up = still a quorum. Losing the zone with 2 plus one more node from another leaves 2 of 5 = no quorum, writes stop (reads may also stop for linearizable ones).

Decision gravity. Cluster size is reversible with membership changes (done carefully, one node at a time). Spreading across zones/regions is a latency decision: cross-region quorum adds the inter-region RTT (50 to 150 ms) to every write.

Everyday analogy. A jury needing 7 of 12: any two groups of 7 must share a juror, so two contradictory verdicts cannot both be "official".

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing 4 nodes "for more safety".
  • Putting a 3-node cluster in 2 zones: losing the zone with 2 nodes kills quorum. Use 3 zones.
  • Mixing up consensus quorums with R + W > N tunable quorums.

notes.title: Split brain
notes.html:
Split brain is when two parts of the system each believe they are the leader and both accept writes, so the data diverges. It usually follows a network partition or a long pause on the old leader.

How it happens: network splits 5 nodes into {A,B} and {C,D,E}. A naive "elect a new leader if the old one is silent" rule lets {C,D,E} elect C while A keeps thinking it is leader. Two leaders, two histories.

Prevention:

  1. Majority rule: only the side with a quorum (3 of 5) may elect a leader and commit. {A,B} cannot make progress.
  2. Terms / epochs: every leadership has an increasing number. Messages from an older term are rejected.
  3. Fencing: protect the resource itself so a zombie leader's writes are refused (see the locks notes).
  4. STONITH (shoot the other node in the head): in classic HA clusters, power off the other node via a management interface before taking over.

Real incident pattern. GitHub's 2018 incident: a 43-second network partition between datacenters made the MySQL orchestrator promote a replica on the other coast while writes had already hit the old primary. Divergent data took about 24 hours to reconcile. Symptom: two primaries reporting read_only=OFF; metric: replication errors and conflicting row versions.

Decision gravity. Choosing strict majority consensus (CP) over "always available" (AP) is a one-way product decision: you decide that the minority side refuses writes. Alternatives: multi-leader with conflict resolution (CRDTs, LWW), accepting merge pain.

Everyday analogy. Two team captains each told "you are in charge" by different managers while the phone line was cut; both give orders and the project forks.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing 2 nodes can be made safe with a heartbeat. Two nodes have no majority; add a witness (3rd node/arbiter).
  • Forgetting the paused-old-leader case (GC pause), not only network partitions.

notes.title: Raft overview: roles and terms
notes.html:
Raft makes consensus understandable by splitting it into: leader election, log replication and safety. Every node is in one of three roles.

  • Follower: passive, replies to leader and candidates.
  • Candidate: a follower that timed out and is asking for votes.
  • Leader: the only one that accepts client writes and replicates them.

Time is divided into terms, numbered 1,2,3... Each term has at most one leader. A node that sees a higher term immediately steps down to follower. Terms act as a logical clock for leadership.

Key persistent state on each node (must survive restarts, stored to disk before replying): currentTerm, votedFor, and the log[] of entries, each tagged with its term.

Typical config (etcd defaults, confirm for your version): heartbeat interval 100 ms, election timeout 1000 ms. Election timeout is randomised per node (e.g. 150 to 300 ms in the Raft paper) so that not everyone becomes a candidate at once.

Industry examples. etcd, Consul, TiKV (one Raft group per region), CockroachDB (per range), RabbitMQ quorum queues, Kafka KRaft controller.

Everyday analogy. A classroom: one student is class monitor (leader) for a term; if the monitor goes silent, someone raises a hand to be elected; a new term number starts every election.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking clients can write to any node. Writes go through the leader (followers redirect).
  • Forgetting that currentTerm and votedFor must be persisted before responding.

notes.title: Raft leader election step by step
notes.html:
A follower that hears nothing from a leader for one election timeout becomes a candidate and asks for votes.

Steps:

  1. Follower times out (random 150 to 300 ms, say). It increments currentTerm (term 4 -> 5), votes for itself, becomes candidate.
  2. It sends RequestVote(term=5, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm) to all peers.
  3. A peer grants its vote if: the candidate's term >= its own, it has not voted in this term, AND the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own (compare last log term first, then last log index).
  4. With a majority of votes, the candidate becomes leader and immediately sends heartbeats (empty AppendEntries) to assert authority.
  5. If votes split (no majority), the timeout expires again with fresh random delays; a new term starts.

Worked example. 5 nodes, leader N1 dies at term 4. N2 (timeout 180 ms) and N5 (timeout 210 ms) time out. N2 starts first, gets votes from N3 and N4 (and itself) = 3 of 5, becomes leader in term 5 before N5's timer fires. Total unavailability about 180 ms plus a round trip. With a 1000 ms election timeout it would be about 1 to 2 s.

Why the log check. It guarantees a leader always has all committed entries ("leader completeness"). A node missing committed data cannot win.

Real incident pattern. Too short an election timeout vs network latency or GC pauses causes constant elections: etcd logs "leader changed" repeatedly, etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total climbs, writes time out. Fix: raise timeouts, fix disk latency (etcd fsync > 10 ms is a classic cause).

Decision gravity. Election timeout is a reversible tuning knob: shorter means faster failover but more false elections. Rule of thumb: 10x the heartbeat and at least a few multiples of network RTT.

Everyday analogy. The silence in a meeting after the chair leaves: whoever speaks first with a good claim and gets most hands raised becomes chair.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the node with the highest ID wins (that is Bully algorithm, not Raft).
  • Forgetting randomised timeouts exist to avoid split votes.
  • Not mentioning the up-to-date-log restriction.

notes.title: Raft log replication and commit
notes.html:
The leader appends each client command to its log, copies it to followers, and marks it committed once a majority has stored it.

Steps:

  1. Client sends command to the leader.
  2. Leader appends (term, index, command) to its local log (and fsyncs).
  3. Leader sends AppendEntries(term, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries[], leaderCommit) to followers.
  4. A follower checks that its entry at prevLogIndex has term prevLogTerm. If yes it appends and acks; if no it rejects (log mismatch).
  5. When a majority (including the leader) have the entry, the leader advances commitIndex, applies the entry to its state machine and replies to the client.
  6. Followers learn the new leaderCommit in the next AppendEntries and apply too.

On rejection the leader decrements nextIndex for that follower and retries until logs match, then overwrites the follower's conflicting suffix. This is the Log Matching Property: if two logs have an entry with the same index and term, all earlier entries are identical.

Worked example. 3 nodes, fsync 2 ms, same-zone RTT 0.5 ms. Leader fsync 2 ms in parallel with follower round trip (0.5 ms + follower fsync 2 ms), so commit takes about 3 ms. Throughput is limited by disk fsync: batching 100 entries per fsync gives tens of thousands of writes/s. Cross-region with 80 ms RTT: every write costs at least about 80 ms.

Safety rule. A leader only commits entries from its own current term by counting replicas; older-term entries become committed indirectly once a current-term entry above them commits. (This avoids the Figure 8 anomaly in the Raft paper.)

Industry examples. etcd serves Kubernetes state; its write p99 is dominated by disk fsync, which is why etcd needs SSDs. TiKV batches and pipelines Raft messages for throughput.

Decision gravity. Synchronous majority replication is a one-way semantic choice: durability and linearizability at the cost of latency. Async replication (Postgres default) is faster but can lose acknowledged writes on failover.

Everyday analogy. A secretary reads out a decision; it becomes official only after most committee members write it in their own minutes.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the leader waits for ALL followers. A majority is enough; slow followers catch up later.
  • Confusing "appended" with "committed" with "applied".
  • Forgetting that the leader fsyncs before counting its own vote.

notes.title: Raft safety, reads, and membership
notes.html:
Safety guarantee: once an entry is committed, every future leader has it. It follows from majority overlap plus the vote restriction on log up-to-dateness.

Linearizable reads. A leader may be stale (deposed but unaware). Options:

  • Log read: put the read through the log (slow, always correct).
  • ReadIndex: leader notes commitIndex, confirms it is still leader via a heartbeat round to a majority, waits for apply, then reads. etcd uses this by default for linearizable reads.
  • Leader lease: leader trusts time-bounded lease; faster but depends on bounded clock drift.
  • Follower/stale reads: fast, may be old. etcd offers serializable reads for this.

Membership changes. Changing from 3 to 5 nodes at once could create two disjoint majorities. Raft uses either joint consensus (old+new quorums both required during transition) or single-server changes (add or remove one at a time, safe). etcd adds learners (non-voting) first so a new node catches up before it can affect quorum.

Log growth. Logs are compacted with snapshots; a far-behind follower receives InstallSnapshot. etcd snapshots and compacts by revision; unbounded history hits the DB size quota (default 2 GB, confirm for your version) and the cluster goes read-only with "no space".

Everyday analogy. Before the chair announces "the current decision is X", they quickly check with the room that they are still chair.

Common interview traps.

  • Reading from the leader without confirming leadership and calling it linearizable.
  • Adding two voters at once to a 3-node cluster without learner or joint consensus care.
  • Never compacting etcd.

notes.title: Paxos intuition
notes.html:
Paxos is the original consensus algorithm; Raft is essentially a more structured way to build the same guarantee. Single-decree (basic) Paxos agrees on one value using two phases and three roles (proposer, acceptor, learner; one node often plays all).

  • Phase 1 (prepare/promise): proposer picks a unique, increasing number n and sends Prepare(n) to acceptors. An acceptor that has not promised a higher number replies Promise(n) plus the highest-numbered value it already accepted (if any), and promises to ignore proposals below n.
  • Phase 2 (accept/accepted): if the proposer got promises from a majority, it sends Accept(n, v), where v is the value from the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported (the proposer MUST adopt it), or its own value if none. Acceptors accept unless they promised a higher number.
  • The value is chosen when a majority accepted it.

Why it is safe. The rule "adopt the highest already-accepted value" ensures that once a value could have been chosen by a majority, every later proposal will rediscover it through majority overlap.

Liveness problem. Two proposers can keep preempting each other with higher numbers (dueling proposers). Fix: elect a distinguished proposer (leader), which is exactly what Multi-Paxos does: after phase 1 once, the leader runs only phase 2 for each log slot. That is functionally Raft's leader-based replication.

Industry examples. Google Chubby, Spanner (Multi-Paxos per tablet), Apache Cassandra lightweight transactions (Paxos for compare-and-set), Microsoft Azure storage. Raft was designed (Ongaro and Ousterhout) mainly because Paxos was hard to implement correctly.

Decision gravity. Choosing Raft over Paxos for a new system is a pragmatic, mostly reversible library choice; you rarely write either yourself. Use etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul instead of implementing consensus.

Everyday analogy. Bidding rounds with numbered tickets: if anyone already got a "yes" for some value in an earlier round, the next bidder must carry that value forward instead of pushing their own.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing Paxos as "just majority vote". The adopt-highest-accepted rule is the crux.
  • Not knowing Multi-Paxos is what real systems run.
  • Believing you should implement your own consensus.

notes.title: Raft vs Paxos vs ZAB vs others
notes.html:
Raft Multi-Paxos ZAB (ZooKeeper) Viewstamped Replication
Leader Strong, required Distinguished proposer Strong Primary
Log gaps Not allowed (contiguous) Allowed in theory Ordered by zxid Contiguous
Understandability Designed for it Notoriously hard Medium Medium
Used by etcd, Consul, TiKV Spanner, Chubby ZooKeeper Research, some systems

Related but different: Byzantine fault tolerant protocols (PBFT, Tendermint) handle malicious nodes and need 3f+1 nodes to tolerate f faults; crash-fault protocols like Raft need 2f+1. Use BFT only when nodes may lie (blockchains), not inside your own datacenter.

Leaderless alternatives: EPaxos (no single leader, helps wide-area latency), and Dynamo-style quorum systems with weaker guarantees.

Decision gravity. Choosing a managed coordination service (etcd/ZooKeeper) rather than embedding Raft in your application is nearly always right; embedding is a heavy, hard-to-reverse commitment (you own snapshots, membership, upgrades).

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing Byzantine fault tolerance for an internal service.
  • Saying ZooKeeper uses Raft (it uses ZAB).

notes.title: Consensus performance and failure modes in production
notes.html:
Latency and throughput:

  • Write latency is one disk fsync on a majority plus one network round trip. Cross-AZ adds about 1 ms; cross-region adds the inter-region RTT.
  • Throughput is raised by batching entries, pipelining AppendEntries, and sharding: many small Raft groups (CockroachDB ranges, TiKV regions) each with its own leader spread over nodes.

Typical failure symptoms and metrics:

  • Leader flapping: frequent elections; leader_changes counter rising; cause is disk fsync stalls, network jitter, CPU starvation of the leader process.
  • No quorum: writes fail with timeouts; has_leader=0. Cause is losing a majority or a bad zone layout.
  • Slow follower: one lagging node; leader keeps sending, memory grows. Cause is slow disk or network.
  • Disk full or DB size quota: cluster goes read-only (etcd alarm NOSPACE).

Worked example. etcd with SSD: fsync p99 under 10 ms is the guideline; with a shared HDD fsync can hit 100 ms, heartbeats get delayed beyond the 1 s election timeout and leadership churns, taking Kubernetes API writes down.

Everyday analogy. A committee meeting where the chairperson keeps losing their voice: each time, the room has to re-elect and nothing gets decided.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting etcd on shared slow disks or mixing it with noisy neighbours.
  • Scaling a single Raft group by adding nodes instead of sharding groups.
  • Forgetting monitoring: alert on leader changes and fsync latency.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Consensus = agree on a value or ordered log despite crashes; safety always, liveness only when the network is eventually stable (FLP).
  • Majority quorums overlap, so decisions are never lost; use 3 or 5 nodes across 3 failure domains; even sizes add no tolerance.
  • Split brain = two leaders; prevent with majority rule, terms/epochs, fencing, or STONITH. GitHub 2018 is the classic incident.
  • Raft: follower/candidate/leader, terms, randomised election timeouts, up-to-date-log vote rule; commit when a majority stores the entry; ReadIndex for linearizable reads; safe membership changes; snapshots.
  • Paxos: prepare/promise then accept; adopt the highest accepted value; Multi-Paxos adds a leader. Same guarantee as Raft.
  • Crash faults need 2f+1 nodes, Byzantine need 3f+1.
  • In production: use etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul, fast disks, alert on leader changes and fsync latency, shard into many groups for scale.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does consensus solve, and what does the FLP result say about it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks the foundation before you are asked to design a leader election or a metadata store.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Consensus lets several machines agree on one value, or one ordered log of values, even if some crash and messages are delayed. It needs agreement (no two decide differently), validity (the value was proposed) and termination. FLP proves no deterministic algorithm can guarantee all three in a fully asynchronous network with one possible crash, so Raft and Paxos always keep safety and give up guaranteed liveness: they may stall during chaos but never decide wrongly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Use: "exactly one leader", "this config is the truth", "this is the transaction order".
  • Replicated state machine: consensus orders the log, every node applies the same commands in the same order, so all reach the same state.
  • Practical liveness: with randomized timeouts, eventually the network is stable enough to elect a leader.
  • Real systems: etcd and Consul (Raft), ZooKeeper (ZAB), Chubby and Spanner (Paxos), Kafka KRaft (Raft).
Client -> Leader -> replicate log entry -> majority acks -> commit
                                  \-> Node1, Node2, Node3 apply same order

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Consensus for everything": many systems avoid it for availability (Dynamo-style, CRDTs).
  • Not knowing the minority side of a partition cannot make progress (CAP).
  • Reading FLP as "consensus is impossible"; it says guaranteed termination is, in a pure async model.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do real systems get around FLP? -> Timeouts and randomization give practical liveness; safety never depends on timing.
  2. Consensus vs replication? -> Plain primary-backup replication can lose or fork data on failover; consensus defines who is leader safely.
  3. When would you avoid consensus? -> High-throughput, geo-distributed writes where eventual consistency is acceptable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior: "it's how nodes agree". Senior: safety vs liveness split, replicated state machine, cost of majority writes, and that you consume it via etcd/ZooKeeper rather than build it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Kubernetes control plane availability is etcd's quorum availability.

questions.promptHtml: Why do consensus clusters use majority quorums and odd sizes? Why is a 4-node cluster no better than 3?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic sizing question; reveals whether you understand the overlap argument.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A majority is floor(N/2)+1. Any two majorities share at least one node, so a new decision always overlaps the previous one and learns about it; that overlap is the safety argument. 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 4 also tolerate only 1 (majority is 3), so the fourth node adds cost and write latency but no tolerance. I use 3 or 5 nodes spread across 3 failure domains.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
N Majority Failures tolerated
3 2 1
4 3 1
5 3 2
7 4 3
  • More nodes means more acks per write and more chatter, so writes get slower.
  • Do not confuse with tunable quorums: with N replicas, write quorum W and read quorum R, R + W > N makes reads overlap writes (N=3, W=2, R=2). Different guarantee from consensus.
  • Spread: a 5-node cluster across zones as 2,2,1 survives losing any one zone; the 3-node cluster in 2 zones (2+1) does not survive the zone with 2.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Picking 4 "for more safety".
  • 3 nodes in 2 zones.
  • Mixing consensus quorums with R + W > N.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not 6 nodes? -> Majority 4 tolerates 2, same as 5; one extra node, no benefit.
  2. What does cross-region placement cost? -> Every write waits for the quorum RTT, 50 to 150 ms.
  3. Can I scale writes by adding nodes? -> No, it slows them; shard into multiple groups.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior recites the formula. Senior explains overlap, failure-domain placement and the latency cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Outages of "3-node cluster across 2 AZs" when the 2-node AZ went down.

questions.contextHtml: Your 3-node etcd cluster runs in two availability zones: etcd-1 and etcd-2 in zone A, etcd-3 in zone B. At 14:02 zone A loses power. Kubernetes API calls start failing: etcdserver: request timed out. From etcd-3: etcdctl endpoint health returns unhealthy: failed to commit proposal: context deadline exceeded. Workloads already running on nodes in zone B keep serving traffic. Management asks: "we had a replica in zone B, why is the cluster down?"
questions.promptHtml: Explain, restore service, and fix the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Force etcd-3 to become leader." It misses that quorum needs 2 of 3 and risks data loss.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is zone A really gone or just partitioned? Is the zone A data disk intact? When was the last backup/snapshot? Can new nodes be created in zone B or C?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not rewrite membership casually. Best case: bring zone A back. If not, restore quorum safely: either start a replacement member that can join (needs a quorum to add, so not possible) or use disaster recovery: etcdctl snapshot restore from the latest snapshot or --force-new-cluster on etcd-3, accepting loss of anything not on etcd-3.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: quorum lost (1 of 3 up); zone B network issue (less likely); etcd-3 disk problem. Red herring: workloads still serve because the data plane does not need the API server.
  4. How I'd verify each: etcdctl endpoint status -w table from etcd-3 (does it show a leader?); check etcd_server_has_leader and logs for "lost leader".
  5. Root cause: 3 nodes across 2 zones makes zone A hold a majority; losing it removes quorum.
  6. Fix: Short term: recover per above, then add new members back and a fresh snapshot. Long term: 3 nodes in 3 zones (1/1/1), or 5 nodes 2/2/1.
  7. Prevention: Failure-domain spread check in provisioning; regular snapshot restore drills; alert on has_leader == 0.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: --force-new-cluster can lose acknowledged writes and splits history if zone A returns later with old data; do it only when zone A is truly dead. Three zones add some write latency (about 1 ms cross-AZ).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would 4 nodes (2+2) help? -> No: majority 3, losing a zone of 2 leaves 2, no quorum.
  • Why were reads still working in zone B pods? -> Already-running pods and kubelets do not need etcd; new scheduling and changes are what fail.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rushed --force-new-cluster brought the cluster back in minutes but silently dropped the last few seconds of writes; a second zone returning with an old data directory nearly re-joined and had to be wiped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tries to make the single node leader.
  • Hire: explains quorum math and plans DR plus 3-zone layout.
  • Strong hire: weighs data-loss risk of forcing, snapshot recency, drills, and alerting.

questions.contextHtml: A team says: "We have a Postgres primary and one standby in two datacenters. We want automatic failover: if the standby sees no heartbeat from the primary for 10 s it promotes itself. Management wants zero data loss and no downtime." Last quarter a network cut lasting 40 s between the datacenters happened; the primary was healthy and serving clients in DC1 the whole time.
questions.promptHtml: What happens in the next cut, and what would you ask and propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the heartbeat timeout." It does not solve the two-node problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the RPO/RTO truly required? Can clients reach both DCs during the cut? Is a third site available for a witness? Replication sync or async?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable automatic promotion for now (manual failover with a human check) until a witness exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: with 2 nodes, the standby cannot tell "primary dead" from "I am partitioned"; promoting creates two primaries.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test in staging: block traffic between nodes and watch which side promotes; check whether clients can still reach the old primary.
  5. Root cause: Two nodes have no majority; a heartbeat cannot prove death.
  6. Fix: Add a third voter (witness/arbiter in a third site) and require quorum for promotion; fence the old primary (STONITH, revoke its network or storage, or make it demote itself when it loses quorum). Use a tested HA tool built on a consensus store (etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper-backed, e.g. Patroni; verify setup).
  7. Prevention: Failover game days with partition injection; alert when two nodes report pg_is_in_recovery() = false.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Zero data loss needs synchronous replication to at least one other node, which costs latency and can stall writes if the standby is down. "Zero downtime and zero data loss" in a partition is impossible (CAP); I would ask management which to give up.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Old primary is paused by GC and wakes after promotion? -> Fencing; it must be unable to write (token/epoch check or power off).
  • Witness in the same DC as the primary? -> Then it fails together with it; the witness must be a separate failure domain.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promotion during a 43-second inter-DC partition led to two primaries accepting writes; reconciling the divergent rows took a day, which is the pattern of the well-known 2018 GitHub incident.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes timeouts.
  • Hire: needs a third voter and fencing.
  • Strong hire: raises CAP trade-off with management, sync replication cost, game days.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through a Raft leader election after the leader dies. Why are election timeouts randomized, and why is there a log check on votes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard Raft question; separates memorizers from people who know the safety reasons.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A follower that hears no heartbeat for its election timeout increments its term, votes for itself and sends RequestVote(term, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm). A peer votes yes if the term is at least its own, it has not voted this term, and the candidate's log is at least as up to date. A majority makes it leader and it sends heartbeats immediately. Timeouts are randomized so nodes do not all become candidates together and split the votes. The log check guarantees a leader already holds every committed entry.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1. Timeout (say 150 to 300 ms), term 4 to 5, vote for self.
  2. RequestVote to peers.
  3. Grant rule: term >= own, votedFor empty or same candidate, candidate log up to date (last log term first, then last index).
  4. Majority: leader sends empty AppendEntries as heartbeat.
  5. Split vote: no majority, timers expire again, new term.
  • Persistence: currentTerm and votedFor are written to disk before replying, or a restarted node could vote twice in a term.
  • Unavailability is about the election timeout plus an RTT (about 180 ms in the example vs 1 to 2 s with a 1,000 ms timeout).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Highest ID wins" (that is the Bully algorithm).
  • Forgetting randomization or the up-to-date restriction.
  • Not persisting votedFor.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a partitioned node keeps incrementing its term? -> On rejoin its high term disrupts the cluster; Pre-Vote (an optional extension) avoids this.
  2. How do you set the election timeout? -> Heartbeat x ~10 and several network RTTs; too short causes flapping.
  3. Can two leaders exist? -> At most one per term; an old leader steps down when it sees a higher term.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior lists the steps. Senior ties each rule to a safety property and mentions persistence, Pre-Vote and tuning.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Election timeouts shorter than disk stalls cause leader flapping in etcd (Q018).

questions.contextHtml: A 3-node etcd cluster backing a Kubernetes cluster shows API timeouts every few minutes. etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total rose by 14 in the last hour. Logs: etcdserver: failed to send out heartbeat on time (exceeded the 100ms timeout for 412ms) and slow fdatasync took 1.3s. etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds p99 is 180 ms. CPU on nodes is 20%. A nightly backup job uploads a 4 GB file from the same volume. Heartbeat is 100 ms and election timeout 1000 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. Which signals are red herrings?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase CPU." CPU is at 20%; the data shows disk latency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the data dir on a dedicated SSD? Does flapping line up with the backup window? Any recent growth in write rate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the backup job and move it off this volume or throttle it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) fsync stalls from shared disk contention; (b) network jitter between nodes; (c) noisy neighbour on the VM; (d) etcd DB too large. CPU is a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds and etcd_disk_backend_commit_duration_seconds vs backup timestamps; iostat -x 1 for await and %util; etcdctl check perf; ping RTT between members.
  5. Root cause: The leader's WAL fsync (needed before it counts its own vote and replies) is stalled by the large sequential backup write, so heartbeats are late; followers time out and elect, repeatedly.
  6. Fix: Short term: stop the backup. Long term: dedicate a low-latency SSD to etcd, take snapshots with etcdctl snapshot save on a schedule off the data volume, aim for fsync p99 under 10 ms.
  7. Prevention: Alert on leader changes > 3/hour and fsync p99 > 10 ms; disk performance is a provisioning check.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise the election timeout to 10 s as the main fix: failover becomes 10 s slow and the disk problem remains. A modest increase can be a stopgap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would moving to 5 nodes help? -> No, slower commits and the same disk issue.
  • What if fsync is fine but heartbeat late? -> Check CPU throttling (cgroup limits), GC, or network.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" log shipper on the etcd volume produced the same symptom every night at 02:00; the pattern was only visible after overlaying cron times on the fsync graph.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales CPU/nodes.
  • Hire: ties fsync latency to heartbeat misses and fixes the disk.
  • Strong hire: explains why the leader fsync gates commit, proposes alerts and sane timeout tuning.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate wrote a toy Raft RequestVote handler. In a chaos test, two nodes both won term 7, and a node that crashed and restarted voted for a second candidate in the same term. Find every bug.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
synchronized boolean handleRequestVote(long term, String candidateId,
                                       long lastLogIndex, long lastLogTerm) {
    if (term < currentTerm) return false;
    if (votedFor == null) {
        votedFor = candidateId;          // in memory only
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}
@Synchronized
fun handleRequestVote(term: Long, candidateId: String,
                      lastLogIndex: Long, lastLogTerm: Long): Boolean {
    if (term < currentTerm) return false
    if (votedFor == null) {
        votedFor = candidateId          // in memory only
        return true
    }
    return false
}
questions.promptHtml: List the bugs and the corrected logic.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices only the missing log check; misses persistence and term handling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where is currentTerm updated? Is state written to disk (fsync) before the reply is sent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop using it for anything real; reproduce with a deterministic simulator.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) votedFor not persisted, so after a restart it is null and the node votes again in the same term; (b) no up-to-date log check, so a stale candidate can win and committed entries can be lost; (c) when a higher term arrives, currentTerm is not updated and votedFor is not reset, so the node ignores later elections or never votes in the new term; (d) not idempotent: a retransmitted request from the same candidate should still get a yes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Jepsen-style or deterministic tests: kill -9 between vote and reply; inject a stale-log candidate; check leader uniqueness per term.
  5. Root cause: The vote handler ignores three safety rules: persistence, term adoption, and log up-to-dateness.
  6. Fix: see code below: adopt higher term (reset votedFor), grant only if log up to date and votedFor is null or the same candidate, persist term and vote before replying.
  7. Prevention: Model-check the protocol (TLA+ spec of Raft exists), property tests for "at most one leader per term" and "leader completeness".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hand-roll Raft in production; use etcd or a mature library. fsync per vote costs latency, but elections are rare.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
synchronized boolean handleRequestVote(long term, String cand, long lastIdx, long lastTerm) {
    if (term < currentTerm) return false;
    if (term > currentTerm) { currentTerm = term; votedFor = null; role = FOLLOWER; }
    boolean logOk = lastTerm > log.lastTerm()
        || (lastTerm == log.lastTerm() && lastIdx >= log.lastIndex());
    if (logOk && (votedFor == null || votedFor.equals(cand))) {
        votedFor = cand;
        persist(currentTerm, votedFor);   // fsync BEFORE replying
        return true;
    }
    persist(currentTerm, votedFor);
    return false;
}
@Synchronized
fun handleRequestVote(term: Long, cand: String, lastIdx: Long, lastTerm: Long): Boolean {
    if (term < currentTerm) return false
    if (term > currentTerm) { currentTerm = term; votedFor = null; role = Role.FOLLOWER }
    val logOk = lastTerm > log.lastTerm() ||
        (lastTerm == log.lastTerm() && lastIdx >= log.lastIndex())
    if (logOk && (votedFor == null || votedFor == cand)) {
        votedFor = cand
        persist(currentTerm, votedFor)   // fsync BEFORE replying
        return true
    }
    persist(currentTerm, votedFor)
    return false
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why compare last log term before index? -> A longer log from an old term may contain uncommitted junk; term order tells which log is more recent.
  • Candidate in higher term with stale log? -> The voter adopts the term but refuses the vote.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A custom replication layer skipped the vote persistence "for speed" and a rolling restart produced two leaders in one term for a few hundred ms, enough to double-apply a batch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: finds one bug.
  • Hire: finds persistence, log check, term handling.
  • Strong hire: also idempotence, testing approach, advises against rolling own.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't a Raft leader just answer reads from its local state? How do ReadIndex and leader leases fix it, and what does each cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know that writes through consensus do not make reads safe by themselves.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A leader may have been deposed by a partition and not know it, so a local read can return stale data and violate linearizability. ReadIndex records the commit index, confirms leadership with a heartbeat round to a majority, waits until that index is applied, then reads: one network round trip but no log write. A leader lease skips the round by trusting a time-bounded lease, which is faster but depends on bounded clock drift. Follower or serializable reads are fastest but may be stale.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Log read: put the read in the log; always correct, slowest (disk + replication).
  • ReadIndex: leader notes commitIndex, heartbeats a majority to prove it is still leader, waits for appliedIndex >= readIndex, serves. etcd uses it for linearizable reads by default.
  • Lease read: leader may serve locally while its lease (derived from the last majority heartbeat, shorter than the election timeout minus drift) is valid. Risk: clock drift or a paused leader beyond the lease.
  • Follower reads: a follower can ask the leader for a read index then serve itself, spreading load; or serve stale (serializable in etcd).
Client -> Leader: read k
Leader: readIndex = commitIndex (41)
Leader -> majority: heartbeat (am I still leader?)  -> ok
Leader: wait applied >= 41, then read k

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Serving reads from the leader without confirming leadership and calling them linearizable.
  • Trusting lease reads when the VM can be paused.
  • Using stale reads for authorization decisions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does throughput change? -> ReadIndex amortizes: one heartbeat round can confirm many queued reads.
  2. What happens in a partition with the old leader? -> It cannot reach a majority, so ReadIndex fails; a lease read might still answer until the lease expires.
  3. When are stale reads fine? -> Dashboards and caches where bounded staleness is acceptable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Junior: "read from the leader". Senior: the deposed-leader hazard, three mechanisms with cost and assumption of each.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service that used serializable (stale) etcd reads for lock checks observed a lock holder that no longer existed.

questions.contextHtml: Your 3-node etcd cluster (nodes e1, e2, e3, e1 is leader) serves 4,000 writes/s. You are replacing e2's failing disk and growing to 5 nodes (add e4 and e5) in the same maintenance, without downtime. A colleague proposes: "add e4 and e5 simultaneously with member add, then remove e2." Current DB size is 1.4 GB.
questions.promptHtml: Is that plan safe? Give the safe plan and the risks.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sure, add both and wait." It does not see the quorum risk of unready members.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is e2 healthy enough to stay until replacement is ready? What is the current backup status? Are e4/e5 in distinct zones? Network bandwidth for snapshot transfer?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Take a fresh snapshot first (etcdctl snapshot save) as a rollback.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: adding two voters at once raises the quorum from 2 of 3 to 3 of 5 while they have empty logs; if e1 then fails, only e3 plus two empty nodes remain, and unready members count against availability. Adding as learners avoids this.
  4. How I'd verify each: etcdctl endpoint status -w table for leader and index; etcdctl member list showing learner flag; check raft_index catch-up.
  5. Root cause of the risk: Membership changes alter the voting set; an uncaught-up voter can make quorum depend on a node that cannot yet contribute.
  6. Fix (plan): (a) etcdctl member add e4 --learner, start e4, wait until caught up; (b) etcdctl member promote <id>; (c) repeat for e5, one at a time; (d) only then remove e2 (member remove) since the cluster is already healthy at 5; (e) verify health after each step. Raft itself offers joint consensus or single-server changes for safety.
  7. Prevention: Runbook and automated checks "cluster healthy before each step"; do changes one member at a time.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Going 3 to 5 adds write latency (more acks, majority 3) and snapshot traffic; I would not change membership during an incident or while a member is unhealthy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• e1 dies mid-process? -> If e3 and e2 form quorum (2 of 3) the cluster continues; stop the change until stable.
  • Why learners? -> Non-voting, replicate logs, so they cannot affect quorum until promoted.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rolling replacement that removed a member before its replacement caught up left two voters and zero slack; one more failure would have meant restoring from snapshot.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves the plan.
  • Hire: serial adds with learners.
  • Strong hire: explains quorum change arithmetic, snapshot backup, health gates, latency impact.

questions.contextHtml: A metadata service runs one 3-node Raft group (same region, RTT 0.5 ms, SSD fsync 2 ms) at 3,000 writes/s, p99 commit 9 ms. Product expects 10x growth to 30,000 writes/s and a second region with 80 ms RTT to the existing one. Proposal 1: "add 4 more nodes to the group for capacity." Proposal 2: shard into many Raft groups. Data is 400 GB.
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate both, show the math, and say what happens with the second region.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "More nodes means more capacity." In Raft more voters means more acks, not more write throughput.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the workload key-partitionable? Do operations span keys (transactions)? Is the second region for latency or DR? Read/write ratio?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Batch and pipeline: one fsync can cover many entries; at 2 ms per fsync and no batching the ceiling is about 500 fsyncs/s, with batches of 100 it is about 50,000 entries/s on paper.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the single leader's disk and CPU is the limit; adding voters raises needed acks (majority 4 of 7) and slows commits; sharding spreads leaders across nodes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test: commit latency vs batch size, leader CPU, fsync histogram; per-group throughput.
  5. Root cause of the limit: Every write goes through one leader log in order; capacity of a group is the capacity of one leader.
  6. Fix: Shard into, say, 32 ranges (about 12 GB each), each its own 3-replica Raft group with leaders spread across nodes (the CockroachDB/TiKV model); batch and pipeline AppendEntries. Cross-range transactions need a coordination protocol (2PC over groups), which adds cost.
  7. Prevention: Monitor per-group leader balance and hot ranges; cap range size and split automatically.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Second region: a quorum that spans regions makes every write cost at least the 80 ms RTT (client sequential throughput about 12 writes/s per connection; need concurrency). Alternative: keep quorum in one region and use async followers in region 2 (fast, but can lose recent writes on failover) or per-range leaseholder placement near the writers. I would not stretch one group across regions without a latency budget.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Hot key? -> Sharding does not help one key; need splitting the key or caching/batching.
  • Cross-shard transactions? -> 2PC with each participant a Raft group; latency is two consensus rounds.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added nodes to scale a coordination service and writes got slower; the fix was fewer nodes per group and many more groups.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: add nodes.
  • Hire: shard into groups, batching math.
  • Strong hire: cross-region trade-offs, hot ranges, 2PC cost, async follower alternative.

questions.contextHtml: You will build a configuration store used by services in three regions (US 80 ms from EU, 150 ms from AP, 200 ms EU to AP; illustrative). It stores 50 MB of config, 200 writes/s, strongly consistent reads wanted. The team debates: (A) embed a Raft library in the service, 5 voters 2/2/1; (B) run etcd or Consul as a managed dependency; (C) a leaderless protocol like EPaxos; (D) Byzantine-tolerant PBFT "for safety".
questions.promptHtml: Which do you recommend? Reason about the latency of a write issued in AP.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks the most exotic one, or ignores that the leader's location sets the latency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are writes rare (config) or frequent? Is stale read acceptable for most reads? RPO/RTO requirement? Who operates it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a leader-based group puts writes through one leader: with the leader in US, an AP write pays 150 ms to the leader plus the leader's commit RTT to the nearest voters (e.g. 80 ms to EU if it holds the second US node's majority, or less with 2 US voters: majority 3 of 5 = 2 US + 1 EU, so about 80 ms): about 230 ms.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure with the real network; test leader failover time; check read patterns.
  5. Root cause of latency: physics: one round to leader plus one round to a majority.
  6. Fix / recommendation: (B) a managed etcd/Consul with leader placed in the busiest region, 5 voters 2/2/1; use serializable or follower reads for most config reads (cached locally) and linearizable reads only when needed. 200 writes/s and 50 MB are tiny for etcd.
  7. Prevention: Client-side caching with watches; failover drills; monitoring of quorum and leader location.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: (A) embedding means owning snapshots, membership changes, upgrades: heavy, hard to reverse. (C) EPaxos can lower wide-area latency but is complex and rare in production. (D) BFT needs 3f+1 nodes and is for untrusted participants, not our own datacenters. This is mostly a reversible choice if hidden behind a client interface.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Region US goes down? -> 5 voters 2/2/1: losing US (2) leaves 3, still a quorum; a new leader is elected (~1 to 2 s with default timeouts).
  • Must AP writes be faster? -> Move the leader, or accept per-region config with async replication for non-critical keys.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" in-house Raft library for a config service outlived its authors; every upgrade needed a heroic manual snapshot dance.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks by novelty.
  • Hire: picks managed etcd/Consul with justification.
  • Strong hire: latency math for AP writes, read strategies, failover math, rejects BFT and embedding with reasons.

questions.contextHtml: At 03:10 a Kubernetes cluster stopped accepting changes: etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded. Existing pods kept running. etcdctl alarm list shows memberID:... alarm:NOSPACE. etcdctl endpoint status shows DB size 2.1 GB (quota 2 GB, default; verify for your version), 3 members, healthy leader. Disk free is 70%. Over the last week DB size rose from 400 MB to 2.1 GB. Root cause found later: a controller rewrote a status field of 50,000 objects every second after a bug.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review: timeline of actions to recover, root cause, and action items.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the quota" as the only fix, and "disk is free so it is not a space problem".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is auto-compaction enabled? When did the last defrag run? Which objects/keys grew? Do we have a recent snapshot?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the hot-looping controller (scale to 0) so writes stop. Take a snapshot first. Then: get the current revision (etcdctl endpoint status -w json), etcdctl compact <rev>, etcdctl defrag one member at a time, etcdctl alarm disarm, verify writes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) MVCC revision history never compacted; (b) write amplification from a buggy controller; (c) large objects or events; red herring: disk free 70% is irrelevant, the limit is the quota.
  4. How I'd verify each: etcdctl endpoint status -w table (DB size vs in-use size), count keys by prefix, etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes vs ..._in_use_in_bytes, audit logs for writer identity.
  5. Root cause: Each update creates a new revision; without compaction the old revisions accumulate until the backend hits the quota; at that point etcd goes read-only (alarm) to protect itself. Compaction frees logical space but defrag returns it to the file.
  6. Fix: Short term as above. Long term: enable auto-compaction (e.g. hourly retention, verify flag for your setup), schedule defrag off-peak, fix the controller to not write unchanged status, set API priority and fairness / rate limits.
  7. Prevention: Alert at 70% of quota, alert on write rate by user agent, dashboard for revision growth; test the runbook.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Raising the quota (etcd recommends keeping it modest, around a few GB; verify) buys time but hides the cause and lengthens defrag and snapshot times. Defrag blocks the member while running; do one at a time, leader last.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did pods keep running? -> Data plane independent of the API for running pods; control actions fail.
  • After compaction the size did not drop? -> Needs defrag.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The same alarm hit at 03:00 for a team whose only runbook step was "restart etcd", which fixes nothing because the alarm persists after restart.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts or raises quota only.
  • Hire: compact, defrag, disarm, find the writer.
  • Strong hire: blameless timeline, alerts, auto-compaction, rate limiting, runbook drill.
